A fortiori: With even stronger reason—if one fact is true, a second related fact must also be true.
A mensa et thoro: From table and bed—referring to legal separation without divorce.
A posteriori: From later—reasoning derived from observation and experience after an event.
A priori: From earlier—reasoning derived from general principles before examining facts.
A quo: From which—referring to the lower court from which an appeal is taken.
Ab extra: From outside—concerning funding or information received from a third party.
Ab incunablis: From infancy—from the very beginning or birth.
Ab initio: From the beginning—void or invalid from the outset.
Ab intra: From within—arising from inside a person or entity.
Absoluta sententia expositore non indige: An absolute judgment needs no expositor—clear language requires no interpretation.
Absque hoc: Without this—the negative part of a plea at common law.
Abundans cautela non nocet: Abundant caution does no harm—excessive care is not prejudicial.
Accessorium non ducit sed sequitur suum: An accessory does not draw, but follows its principal—accessory liability follows the principal.
Accessorius sequitur: One who is an accessory to a crime cannot be guilty of a more serious crime than the principal offender.
Acta exteriora indicant interiora secret: Outward acts indicate the inward intent—a person's actions reveal their intentions.
Actio non accrevit infra sex annos: The action has not accrued within six years—statute of limitations defense.
Actio non datur non damnificato: An action is not given to one who is not injured—no injury, no cause of action.
Actio personalis moritur cum persona: A personal action dies with the person—certain claims do not survive the death of the party.
Actionable per se: The very act itself is punishable—no proof of damage is required.
Actori incumbit onus probandi: The burden of proof lies on the plaintiff—the one who asserts must prove.
Actus legis nemini facit injuriam: The act of the law does injury to no one—the law is impartial and does not intend harm.
Actus non facit reum nisi mens sit rea: An act does not make one guilty unless there is a guilty mind—both act and intent are required for criminal liability.
Actus reus: A guilty act—the physical element of a crime.
Ad absurdum: To the point of absurdity—reducing an argument to its most extreme logical conclusion.
Ad ea quae frequentius acciduunt jura ad: Laws are adapted to those cases which occur most frequently.
Ad eundem: To the same level or degree.
Ad hoc: For this purpose—created or arranged for a specific purpose.
Ad hominem: To the person—an argument directed against the person rather than the issue.
Ad idem: Of the same mind—in agreement or consensus.
Ad nauseam: To a disgusting extent—repeated to the point of annoyance.
Ad quaestionem facti non respondent judi: Judges do not answer questions of fact—juries decide facts, judges decide law.
Ad valorem: According to value—a tax or duty based on the value of goods.
Addendum: A thing to be added—an addition to a document.
Aedificare in tuo proprio solo non licet: It is not lawful to build on one's own land what may be injurious to another—property rights are not absolute.
Aequitas legem sequitur: Equity follows the law—equity operates within the framework of the law.
Aequitas nunquam contravenit legem: Equity never contradicts the law—equity supplements but does not override the law.
Affidavit: A sworn written statement usable as evidence in court.
Agenda: Things to be done—a list of items for consideration.
Alibi: Elsewhere—a defense claiming the accused was at another place when the crime occurred.
Alienatio rei praefertur juri accrescend: Alienation is preferred by law over accumulation—the law favors the transfer of property over the right of survivorship.
Aliunde: From elsewhere or from another source—evidence from an external source.
Allegans contraria non est audiendus: One making contradictory statements is not to be heard—inconsistent pleadings are not allowed.
Allegans suam turpitudinem non est audie: One alleging his own infamy is not to be heard—a person cannot benefit from their own wrongdoing.
Allegatio contra factum non est admitten: An allegation contrary to a deed is not to be heard—evidence cannot contradict a written instrument.
Alter ego: Other self—a second identity or closely associated person or entity.
Ambiguitas contra stipulatorem est: An ambiguity is construed against the party using it—contracts are interpreted against the drafter.
Ambiguitas verborum patens nulla verific: A patent ambiguity is never helped by averment—obvious ambiguity cannot be explained by extrinsic evidence.
Amicus curiae: Friend of the court—a person who provides information to assist the court.
Amicus omnibus, amicus nemini: A friend to everyone is a friend to none—one cannot be all things to all people.
Angliae jura in omni casu libertati dant: The laws of England favor liberty in every case.
Animo testandi: With the intention of making a will.
Annus luctus: The year of mourning—a period of mourning for a deceased spouse.
Aqua currit et debet currere: Water runs and ought to run—riparian rights include the natural flow of water.
Arbitrium est judicium: An award is a judgment—an arbitrator's decision has the force of a judgment.
Assentio mentium: The meeting of minds—mutual assent required for a contract.
Assignatus utitur jure auctoris: An assignee is clothed with the rights of his assignor—assignment transfers rights.
Audi alteram partem: Hear the other side—no one shall be condemned without being heard.
Bona fide: In good faith—sincere, genuine, without fraud.
Bona vacantia: Goods without an owner—property that has no clear owner and escheats to the state.
Boni judici est ampliare jurisdictionem: It is the duty of a good judge to enlarge his jurisdiction—within limits.
Boni judicis est judicium sine dilatione: It is the duty of a good judge to cause execution to issue without delay.
Casus fortuitus non est sperandus: A fortuitous event is not to be expected—the law does not anticipate accidents.
Casus omissus pro omisso habendus est: A case omitted is to be held as omitted—what is not included in a statute is excluded.
Caveat: Let him beware—a formal warning or notice.
Caveat emptor: Let the buyer beware—the buyer assumes the risk of quality.
Caveat venditor: Let the seller beware—the seller is responsible for defects.
Cessante causa, cessat effectus: When the cause ceases, the effect ceases—the effect ends with its cause.
Cessante ratione legis, cessat ipsa lex: When the reason for a law ceases, the law itself ceases.
Clausula: A clause—a distinct part of a legal document.
Clausula rebus sic stantibus: Things standing thus—treaties are binding as long as circumstances remain the same.
Codex: A code—a systematic collection of laws.
Comitas gentium: Comity of nations—courts of one jurisdiction recognize the laws of another.
Communis error facit jus: Common error makes law—a long-standing error can become legally recognized.
Compensatio lucri cum damno: Compensation of profit with loss—profits and losses may be set off against each other.
Concordare leges legibus: To harmonize laws with laws—laws should be interpreted consistently.
Condicio sine qua non: A condition without which not—an indispensable condition or essential requirement.
Consensus ad idem: Agreement to the same thing—mutual assent in contracts.
Consensus facit legem: Consent makes the law—agreement creates binding obligations.
Consentientes et agentes poenam non pati: Those consenting and acting do not suffer punishment—consent is a defense to certain acts.
Consideratio: Consideration—something of value exchanged for a promise.
Consuetudo: Custom—established practice that has the force of law.
Consuetudo est altera lex: Custom is another law—custom has the force of law.
Contemporanea expositio est optima et fo: Contemporaneous exposition is the best and strongest in law—contemporary interpretation is most reliable.
Contra bonos mores: Against good morals—contrary to accepted moral standards.
Contra non valentem agere non currit pra: Prescription does not run against one who is unable to act—statute of limitations does not apply to those under legal disability.
Contra proferentem: Against the offeror—ambiguous terms are construed against the party who drafted them.
Corpus delicti: The body of the crime—the essential elements of a crime.
Corpus juris: The body of law—a complete collection of laws.
Corrigenda: Things to be corrected—a list of errors to be corrected.
Crimen falsi: Crime of falsity—the crime of fraud or forgery.
Culpa: Fault or negligence—blameworthiness or breach of duty.
Cum onere: With the burden—property taken subject to existing encumbrances.
Cum privilegio: With privilege—having special rights or exemptions.
Cum testamento annexo: With the will annexed—when an executor is appointed by the court.
Curia advisari vult: The court wishes to be advised—court reserves judgment.
Curiosa et captiosa: Curious and captious—inquiries that are overly technical.
Damnum absque injuria: Damage without injury—damage without legal wrong.
Damnum fatale: Fatal damage—loss caused by inevitable accident.
De bonis asportatis: Of goods carried away—referring to the carrying away of goods.
De bonis non: Of goods not—referring to administration of assets not yet administered.
De facto: In fact—existing in reality, whether lawful or not.
De fide et officio judicis: Concerning the faith and duty of a judge—judicial integrity.
De futuro: Concerning the future—with effect from a future date.
De jure: Concerning the law—by right, legally recognized.
De lege ferenda: Concerning the law to be made—what the law should be.
De lege lata: Concerning the law as it is—existing law.
De minimis non curat lex: The law does not concern itself with trifles—trivial matters are ignored.
De non apparentibus et non existentibus: The same reasoning applies to things not appearing and things not existing—what does not appear is treated as not existing.
De novo: Anew or afresh—trying a matter again as if for the first time.
De son tort: Of his own wrong—a person acting as executor without authority.
Debet esse finis litium: There must be an end to litigation—legal proceedings cannot continue indefinitely.
Debita sequuntur personam debitoris: Debts follow the person of the debtor—a debt is tied to the debtor personally.
Debitor non praesumitur donare: A debtor is not presumed to give—the law does not presume a gift from a debtor.
Decree: A judicial order—a court's final determination.
Dedimus potestatem: We have given power—a commission authorizing someone to act.
Deed: A written legal instrument—a document transferring or confirming title.
Delegata potestas non potest delegari: Delegated power cannot be delegated—one to whom power is delegated cannot sub-delegate.
Delictum: A wrong or offense—a violation of law.
Demesne: Domain—land held in one's own right.
Denatio: A gift or bequest—a testamentary disposition.
Derivativa potestas non potest esse majo: Derivative power cannot be greater than the original—a delegate's power is limited by the delegator's.
Desuetudo: Disuse—the condition of a law that has fallen into disuse.
Detinue: Detention—an action to recover wrongfully detained goods.
Dictum: A saying or statement—an opinion expressed by a judge.
Dignitas: Dignity—the respect owed to the law or to office.
Dolus bonus: Good deceit—a permissible form of deception.
Domesticum: Domestic—relating to the household or family.
Donatio: A gift—a voluntary transfer of property.
Donatio inter vivos: A gift between the living—a gift made during the donor's lifetime.
Donatio mortis causa: A gift in contemplation of death—a gift made in anticipation of death.
Dormit aliquoties lex: The law sometimes sleeps—the law may be temporarily inactive.
Dulcis est lex: The law is sweet—the law is beneficial.
Dura lex, sed lex: The law is harsh, but it is the law—even harsh laws must be obeyed.
Ea est accipienda interpretatio, quae vi: That interpretation is to be accepted which is free from fault—the best interpretation is the one without error.
Ei incumbit probatio qui dicit: The burden of proof lies upon the one who asserts—he who alleges must prove.
Ejusdem generis: Of the same kind—general words following specific ones are limited to the same class.
Electa una via, non datur recursus ad al: When one path is chosen, there is no recourse to another—election of remedies.
Eminent domain: The sovereign right to take private property for public use.
Equality is equity: Equity favors equality—courts of equity strive for equal treatment.
Equity acts in personam: Equity acts upon the person—equitable remedies are directed at persons, not property.
Equity aids the vigilant: Equity helps those who act promptly—laches bars stale claims.
Equity follows the law: Equity operates within and respects the common law.
Equity imputes an intent to fulfill an o: Equity assumes a person intends to perform their duty.
Equity looks to intent rather than form: Equity focuses on substance over technical form.
Equity looks to the substance, not the f: Equity values the substance of a transaction over its form.
Equity never acts in vain: Equity will not make an order that cannot be enforced.
Equity will not suffer a wrong to be wit: Equity provides a remedy for every wrong.
Errores ad sua principia referre est ref: To trace errors to their principles is to refute them.
Error: An error—a mistake in law or fact.
Error in facto: Error in fact—a mistake of fact.
Error in judice: Error in judgment—a mistake by a judge.
Error in lege: Error in law—a mistake of law.
Error juris nocet: Error of law is harmful—mistakes of law are not excused.
Est: Is or are—the third person singular of the verb to be.
Est modus in rebus: There is a measure in all things—everything has its limits.
Estoppel: A bar preventing a party from asserting a fact or right inconsistent with a previous position.
And others—used to refer to additional parties.
Et cetera: And other things—used to indicate additional similar items.
And the following—referring to subsequent sections or pages.
Et uxor: And wife—used in legal documents to include a spouse.
Ex aequo et bono: According to what is equitable and good—deciding based on fairness rather than strict law.
Ex contractu: From a contract—arising out of a contractual relationship.
Ex curia: Out of court—outside the jurisdiction of the court.
Ex delicto: From a wrong—arising from a tort or wrong.
Ex demissione: From the demise—referring to a lease or transfer.
Ex dolo malo non oritur actio: No action arises from fraud—one cannot sue on a fraudulent transaction.
Ex facie: From the face—apparent on the face of the document.
Ex gratia: As a favor—not legally required but done as a kindness.
Ex injuria jus non oritur: Law does not arise from a wrong—illegal acts cannot create legal rights.
Ex maleficio non oritur contractus: A contract does not arise from a wrong—illegal contracts are void.
Ex more: According to custom—in accordance with established practice.
Ex nihilo nihil fit: Nothing comes from nothing—something cannot arise from nothing.
Ex officio: By virtue of office—by reason of holding a particular office.
Ex parte: On one side only—proceedings brought by one party without notice to the other.
Ex post facto: After the fact—a law that retroactively changes the legal consequences of past actions.
Ex propriis: From his own—from one's own resources.
Ex turpi causa non oritur actio: No action arises from a base cause—a person cannot sue on an illegal transaction.
Ex uno disce omnes: From one, learn all—a single example can illustrate a general rule.
Exceptio firmat regulam in casibus non e: The exception confirms the rule in cases not excepted—exceptions prove the general rule.
Exceptio probat regulam de rebus non exc: The exception proves the rule concerning things not excepted.
Executio est finis et fructus legis: Execution is the end and fruit of the law—enforcement completes the legal process.
Executio legis non habet injuriam: The execution of the law does no injury—enforcing the law is not wrongful.
Exempli gratia: For example—used to introduce an illustration.
Exhibit: A document or object presented as evidence in court.
Exoneration: Release from obligation—being freed from a duty or liability.
Expedit rei publicae ne sua re quis male: It is in the public interest that no one use their property badly.
Expressio eorum quae tacite insunt nihil: The expression of things tacitly implied has no effect—stating what is already implied is redundant.
Expressio unius est exclusio alterius: The express mention of one thing excludes others—listing specific items implies exclusion of others.
Expressum facit cessare tacitum: What is expressed makes what is implied cease—explicit terms override implied ones.
Extra legem: Outside the law—not governed by law.
Extra territorium jus dicenti impune non: One who pronounces law outside his territory is not obeyed with impunity.
Extremis: At the end—in the final stage.
Fac et excusa: Do and excuse—act first and justify later.
Factio: A making or doing—the act of creating.
Factum: An act or deed—something that has been done.
Facultas probationum non est angustanda: The right of offering proof is not to be narrowed—evidence should be liberally admitted.
Falsa demonstratio non nocet: A false description does not harm—an incorrect description does not invalidate if the identity is clear.
Falsa grammatica non vitiat chartam: Bad grammar does not vitiate a deed—minor grammatical errors do not invalidate legal documents.
Falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus: False in one thing, false in everything—a witness who lies in one matter may be disbelieved in all.
Fatetur facinus qui judicium fugit: One who flees judgment confesses guilt—flight is evidence of guilt.
Fecit: He made—used in documents to indicate execution.
Felo de se: A felon of himself—one who commits suicide.
Feme covert: A married woman—a woman under the legal authority of her husband.
Feme sole: A single woman—a woman with legal capacity independent of a husband.
Fiat: Let it be done—a formal authorization.
Fiat justitia ruat caelum: Let justice be done though the heavens fall—justice must be pursued regardless of consequences.
Fiat lux: Let there be light—let enlightenment prevail.
Fieri: To be made or done—used in writs.
Fieri facias: That you cause to be made—a writ of execution.
Finis finem litibus imponit: The end imposes an end to litigation—final judgment concludes the dispute.
Finis rei attenditur: The end of the thing is considered—the purpose matters.
Flagrante delicto: In the very act of committing a crime—caught red-handed.
Foedus: A treaty or alliance—a formal agreement between nations.
Forced heir: A person who cannot be disinherited.
Foreclosure: The process by which a mortgagee takes property from a defaulting mortgagor.
Foreseeability: The quality of being foreseeable—a factor in negligence liability.
Forfeiture: Loss of property as a penalty for wrongdoing.
Forgery: The act of falsely making or altering a document with intent to defraud.
Forma pauperis: In the form of a poor person—proceedings allowed without payment of court costs.
Format: A prescribed form—a model or pattern.
Formula: A form or rule—a prescribed method.
Forum: A court or jurisdiction—the place where legal proceedings are held.
Forum conveniens: A convenient forum—the proper court for a case.
Forum non conveniens: An inconvenient forum—a court that is not appropriate to hear a case.
Fraud: Intentional deception to cause someone to part with something of value.
Fraus est celare fraudem: It is a fraud to conceal a fraud—concealing fraud is itself fraudulent.
Fraus latet in generalibus: Fraud lies hidden in generalities—general statements can conceal fraud.
Frustra legis auxilium quaerit qui in le: He who commits a wrong against the law seeks the law's aid in vain.
Frustra petis quod mox es restiturus: You ask in vain for what you will soon restore.
Functus officio: Having discharged its office—a body or person that has completed its duties.
Gabella: A tax or toll—an excise duty.
Gambling: Gaming or wagering—betting on uncertain events.
Garde: Guardianship—the care and custody of a person or property.
Garnishment: A legal proceeding to collect a debt by seizing property in the hands of a third party.
Generalia specialibus non derogant: General things do not derogate from special things—specific provisions prevail over general ones.
Generalis: General—applicable to a class or group.
Generalis clausula non porrigitur ad ea: A general clause does not extend to those things which have been specifically included before.
Gift: A voluntary transfer of property without consideration.
Good faith: Honest intention—acting without fraud or deceit.
Gravamen: The grievance or injury—the essence of a complaint.
Grosso modo: In a general way—roughly or approximately.
Guarantee: A promise to answer for another's debt or performance.
Guardian: A person appointed to care for a minor or incapacitated person.
Habeas corpus: You shall have the body—a writ to bring a prisoner before a court to determine legality of detention.
Hac vice: For this occasion—specifically for this purpose.
Hereditas: Inheritance—property received from a deceased person.
Hereditas damnosa: A burdensome inheritance—property that carries more liabilities than assets.
Hereditas jacens: A lying inheritance—an inheritance not yet accepted.
Homage: A formal acknowledgment of feudal allegiance.
Honorarium: A payment for services rendered, not legally required.
Hostes humani generis: Enemies of the human race—pirates and similar criminals.
Hypotheca: A mortgage or pledge—security for a debt.
Ibidem: In the same place—used in citations.
Id certum est quod certum reddi potest: That is certain which can be made certain—certainty is not required if it can be determined.
Idem sonans: Sound the same—names that sound alike are legally the same.
Ignorantia facti excusat: Ignorance of fact is excusable—mistake of fact can be a defense.
Ignorantia juris neminem excusat: Ignorance of the law excuses no one—everyone is presumed to know the law.
Ignorantia legis non excusat: Ignorance of the law is no excuse.
Illegitimi non carborundum: Don't let the bastards grind you down—a pseudo-Latin phrase.
Impotentia excusat legem: Impotence excuses the law—inability is an excuse.
In absentia: In absence—proceedings conducted without the party present.
In aequali jure: In equal right—on an equal legal footing.
In articulo mortis: At the point of death—in the final moments.
In casu: In the case—in the particular instance.
In commendam: In trust—held for the benefit of another.
In dubio pro reo: In doubt, for the accused—when in doubt, decide in favor of the defendant.
In extremis: At the point of death—in extreme circumstances.
In favorem vitae: In favor of life—interpretations that favor life.
In forma pauperis: In the form of a poor person—proceedings allowed without payment of costs.
In fraudem legis: In fraud of the law—in evasion of the law.
In globo: In a mass—taken as a whole.
In gremio legis: In the bosom of the law—within the protection of the law.
In illo tempore: At that time—at the relevant time.
In loco parentis: In the place of a parent—acting as a parent.
In medias res: Into the middle of things—in the midst of affairs.
In mortua manu: In a dead hand—perpetual ownership by a corporation.
In negotio: In business—in the course of business.
In nuce: In a nutshell—in a concise form.
In pari delicto: In equal fault—both parties equally at fault.
In pari materia: On the same matter—relating to the same subject.
In personam: Against a person—directed at a specific person.
In propria persona: In one's own person—representing oneself in court.
In rem: Against a thing—directed at property rather than a person.
In rerum natura: In the nature of things—in reality.
In solidum: For the whole—jointly and severally liable.
In statu quo: In the state in which it was—in the former condition.
In vino veritas: In wine, truth—people are more truthful when drunk.
Inadimplenti non est adimplendum: To one who does not perform, no performance is due—non-performance excuses the other party.
Incidere: To fall into—to come to pass.
Incidentia: Incidents—things that accompany or are connected.
Incompetence: Lack of legal capacity—inability to act or understand.
Indenture: A formal agreement—a contract between parties.
Infringement: Violation—the unauthorized use of a right.
Iniuria: A legal wrong—an injury to a right.
Iniuria non excusat injuriam: One wrong does not excuse another—two wrongs don't make a right.
Injuria: A wrong or injury—a violation of legal right.
Injuria sine damno: Injury without damage—a violation of right without actual loss.
Inspeximus: We have inspected—a document confirming another.
Insula: An island—a piece of land surrounded by water.
Insurance: A contract to indemnify against loss.
Intellectual property: Creations of the mind—patents, copyrights, trademarks.
Inter partes: Between parties—among the parties to a proceeding.
Intestate: Without a will—dying without a valid will.
Intestatus: Without a will—not having made a will.
Inventory: A list of assets—a detailed catalog.
Ipse dixit: He himself said it—an unsupported assertion.
Ipso facto: By the fact itself—by the very act.
Ipso jure: By the law itself—automatically by operation of law.
Irreparable: Not able to be repaired—beyond remedy.
Judex: A judge—one who presides over a court.
Judex damnatur cum nocens absolvitur: The judge is condemned when the guilty is acquitted.
Judex est lex loquens: The judge is the speaking law—the judge gives voice to the law.
Judicia sunt tanquam juris dicta: Judgments are as the dicta of the law.
Judicial: Relating to courts—pertaining to the administration of justice.
Judiciary: The branch of government that interprets laws.
Jura novit curia: The court knows the law—the judge is presumed to know the law.
Juration: The act of swearing—the taking of an oath.
Jurator: A juror—one who serves on a jury.
Jure divino: By divine right—by the will of God.
Jure humano: By human law—by the law of men.
Jure uxoris: By right of wife—the husband's right through his wife.
Jurisconsult: A legal expert—one skilled in law.
Jurisdiction: The power to hear and decide cases—legal authority.
Jurist: A legal scholar—one learned in law.
Jus accrescendi: The right of survivorship—the right of the surviving joint tenant.
Jus ad rem: A right to a thing—a claim to a specific object.
Jus civile: Civil law—the law of a particular state.
Jus commune: Common law—the general law of the land.
Jus cogens: A compelling law—a peremptory norm of international law.
Jus disponendi: The right of disposition—the power to transfer property.
Jus habendi: The right of possession—the right to hold property.
Jus in personam: A right against a person—a personal right.
Jus in re: A right in a thing—a property right.
Jus possessionis: The right of possession—the right to possess.
Jus praeferendi: The right of preference—the right to be preferred.
Jus primae noctis: The right of the first night—an alleged feudal right.
Jus publicum: Public law—the law governing the state.
Jus relictae: The right of a widow—the widow's share.
Jus relicti: The right of a widower—the widower's share.
Jus soli: Right of the soil—citizenship by place of birth.
Jus tertii: The right of a third party—a right belonging to another.
Jus utendi: The right of use—the right to use property.
Justitium: A suspension of judicial business—a legal holiday.
Lacuna: A gap or omission—a missing part.
Lapsus linguae: A slip of the tongue—a verbal mistake.
Latitat: He lurks—a writ for a person hiding.
Law: A system of rules—the body of legal principles.
Lawsuit: A legal action—a proceeding in court.
Lawyer: A legal professional—one who practices law.
Lease: A contract for use of property—a rental agreement.
Legal tender: Currency that must be accepted for payment.
Legate: One to whom a legacy is given—a beneficiary.
Legislation: The making of laws—the legislative process.
Lex citius tolerare vult privatum damnum: The law prefers to tolerate private loss than public evil.
Lex contractus: The law of the contract—the law governing a contract.
Lex domicilii: The law of the domicile—the law of the place of residence.
Lex fori: The law of the forum—the law of the court where the case is heard.
Lex loci: The law of the place—the local law.
Lex loci actus: The law of the place of the act—the law where the act occurred.
Lex loci contractus: The law of the place of the contract.
Lex loci delicti: The law of the place of the wrong—the law where the wrong occurred.
Lex loci rei sitae: The law of the place where the thing is situated.
Lex necessitatis: The law of necessity—the right to act in an emergency.
Lex non cogit ad impossibilia: The law does not compel the impossible—no one is required to do the impossible.
Lex non curat de minimis: The law does not concern itself with trifles.
Lex non favet delicatorum votis: The law does not favor the wishes of the fastidious.
Lex non intendit aliquid impossibile: The law does not intend anything impossible.
Lex non novit patris, nec maternam: The law does not know a father or mother—the law does not recognize certain family relationships.
Lex non olet: The law does not smell—the law does not concern itself with unpleasantness.
Lex non requirit verificari quod apparet: The law does not require verification of what appears to the court.
Lex patriae: The law of the country—the national law.
Lex posterior derogat priori: The later law repeals the earlier—later statutes prevail over earlier ones.
Lex prospicit, non respicit: The law looks forward, not backward—laws are generally prospective.
Lex rei sitae: The law of the place where the property is situated.
Lex retro non agit: The law does not act retroactively—no retroactive effect.
Lex specialis derogat generali: A special law prevails over a general law—specific provisions override general ones.
Lex talionis: The law of retaliation—an eye for an eye.
Lex terrae: The law of the land—the law of the realm.
Lex uno ore omnes alloquitur: The law speaks to all with one voice—the law is impartial.
Liability: Legal responsibility—the state of being liable.
Libel: A written defamation—a false statement harming reputation.
Liber homo: A free man—a person with legal freedom.
Liberty: Freedom—the right to act without interference.
Lien: A claim on property—a legal right to retain property.
Limitation: A restriction—a limit on rights or actions.
Lis alibi pendens: A suit pending elsewhere—the same case in another court.
Lis pendens: A pending suit—notice of litigation affecting property.
Litigant: A party to a lawsuit—one who is engaged in litigation.
Litigation: A legal action—the process of lawsuit.
Litis contestatio: Joinder of issue—the formal point of dispute.
Locus contractus: The place of the contract—where the contract was made.
Locus delicti: The place of the wrong—where the offense occurred.
Locus poenitentiae: A place of repentance—an opportunity to withdraw.
Locus standi: A place of standing—the right to bring a legal action.
Magna Carta: The Great Charter—the foundational English legal document.
Mala in se: Wrongs in themselves—acts that are inherently evil.
Mala prohibita: Wrongs because prohibited—acts that are wrong because they are prohibited.
Malum prohibitum: Evil because prohibited—wrongful only because prohibited.
Mandamus: We command—a writ compelling an official to act.
Mandant: One who gives a mandate—the principal.
Mandatary: One who receives a mandate—an agent.
Manslaughter: Unlawful killing without malice—homicide without intent.
Maritime law: Law relating to navigation and shipping.
Marriage: A legal union—the institution of matrimony.
Mater familias: The mother of a family—the head of a household.
Maxim: A general legal principle—an established proposition.
Mens sana in corpore sano: A sound mind in a sound body—the ideal of health.
Minor: A person under the age of majority—an infant.
Misdemeanor: A minor crime—an offense less serious than a felony.
Misprision: Concealment—the failure to report a crime.
Misrepresentation: A false statement—a misstatement of fact.
Mistrial: An invalid trial—a trial that has been terminated.
Modus operandi: A method of operation—a pattern of behavior.
Monetizing: Converting to money—turning assets into cash.
Monopoly: Exclusive control—the domination of a market.
Mortgage: A pledge of property as security for a debt.
Motive: The reason for an action—a purpose.
Movant: One who moves—a party making a motion.
Muniment: A title deed—a document proving ownership.
Mutatis mutandis: With the necessary changes—with appropriate alterations.
Nasciturus pro iam nato habetur, quoties: The unborn is considered as already born whenever its benefit is concerned.
Naturalization: The process of becoming a citizen.
Navigable: Able to be navigated—passable by watercraft.
Ne exeat: Let him not depart—a writ preventing departure.
Necessitas non habet legem: Necessity has no law—necessity may justify otherwise unlawful acts.
Negotiation: The process of bargaining—discussion to reach agreement.
Nemo bis punitur pro eodem delicto: No one is punished twice for the same offense—protection against double jeopardy.
Nemo contra factum suum venire potest: No one can come against his own deed—a person cannot contradict their own act.
Nemo dat quod non habet: No one gives what he does not have—a person cannot transfer a better title than they have.
Nemo debet esse judex in propria causa: No one should be a judge in his own cause—no one may judge their own case.
Nemo debet locupletari ex aliena jactura: No one should be enriched from another's loss—unjust enrichment is not allowed.
Nemo est haeres viventis: No one is the heir of a living person—a living person has no heir.
Nemo ex suo delicto meliorem suam condit: No one can improve their condition by their own wrong.
Nemo in propria causa testis esse debet: No one should be a witness in their own cause.
Nemo judex in causa sua: No one is a judge in their own case.
Nemo moriturus praesumitur mentiri: No one about to die is presumed to lie—dying declarations are trusted.
Nemo potest esse tenens et dominus: No one can be both tenant and owner—conflicting interests.
Nemo potest facere per alium quod per se: No one can do through another what they cannot do themselves.
Nemo potest plus juris ad alium transfer: No one can transfer more right to another than they themselves have.
Nemo praesumitur alienam posteritatem su: No one is presumed to have preferred another's posterity to their own.
Nemo praesumitur donare: No one is presumed to make a gift—gifts are not presumed.
Nemo praesumitur esse ingratus: No one is presumed to be ungrateful.
Nemo praesumitur malus: No one is presumed to be bad—everyone is presumed innocent.
Nemo prohibetur pluribus defensionibus u: No one is prohibited from using several defenses.
Nemo punitur pro alieno delicto: No one is punished for the crime of another—no vicarious criminal punishment.
Nemo sibi esse judex vel suis jus dicere: No one should be a judge for himself or give judgment for his own.
Nemo tenetur ad impossibile: No one is bound to do the impossible—impossibility is an excuse.
Nemo tenetur armare adversarium contra s: No one is bound to arm an adversary against himself.
Nemo tenetur seipsum accusare: No one is bound to accuse himself—the right against self-incrimination.
Nihil dat quod non habet: Nothing gives what it does not have—no one can transfer what they don't own.
Nihil est: It is nothing—it has no effect.
Nihil facit: It does nothing—it has no effect.
Nihil habet: He has nothing—he is without means.
Nihil obstat: Nothing stands in the way—official approval.
Nihil quod est contra rationem est licit: Nothing that is contrary to reason is lawful.
Nil debet: He owes nothing—a plea of no debt.
Nolle prosequi: To be unwilling to prosecute—a decision not to proceed.
Nolo contendere: I do not wish to contest—a plea that does not admit but accepts punishment.
Non assumpsit: He did not undertake—a denial of a contract.
Non bis in idem: Not twice in the same—no double jeopardy.
Non constat: It does not appear—it is not established.
Non decet: It is not fitting—it is improper.
Non est: It is not—it does not exist.
Non est factum: It is not my deed—a denial that a document was executed.
Non est inventus: He is not found—cannot be located.
Non judicabit: He shall not judge—lack of jurisdiction.
Non jurat: He does not swear—refusal to swear.
Non licet: It is not lawful—it is prohibited.
Non obstante veredicto: Notwithstanding the verdict—judgment contrary to the verdict.
Non omne quod licet honestum est: Not everything that is lawful is honorable.
Non prosequitur: He does not prosecute—failure to pursue.
Non sequitur: It does not follow—an illogical conclusion.
Non sunt: They are not—they do not exist.
Non tenetur: He is not bound—he is not obligated.
Non vi, sed lege: Not by force, but by law.
Notary: A public officer—one who certifies documents.
Novation: The substitution of a new obligation for an old one.
Noxa caput sequitur: The injury follows the head—liability follows the principal.
Nudum pactum: A naked promise—a promise without consideration.
Nulla poena sine lege: No punishment without law—no crime without a law.
Nullius: Of no one—belonging to no one.
Nullum crimen, nulla poena sine praevia: No crime, no punishment without a previous penal law.
Nullum simile est idem: No similarity is identity—similar things are not identical.
Obit dictum: A saying at death—a remark made just before death.
Obligee: One to whom an obligation is owed—the creditor.
Obligor: One who owes an obligation—the debtor.
Obscurum per obscurius: The obscure by the more obscure—explaining something unclear with something even less clear.
Oligarchy: Rule by a few—government by an elite.
Omne majus continet in se minus: The greater contains in itself the less—the greater includes the lesser.
Omne principale trahit ad se accessorium: The principal draws the accessory to itself—the accessory follows the principal.
Omnis definitio in jure civili periculos: Every definition in civil law is dangerous—definitions can be misleading.
Omnis nova constitutio futuris formam im: Every new law should give form to the future, not the past—no retroactive effect.
Onus probandi: The burden of proof—the obligation to prove.
Op cit: In the work cited—used in references.
Opinio juris: Opinion of law—belief that a practice is legally required.
Oppression: Cruelty—the exercise of authority in an unjust manner.
Overrule: To set aside—to reverse a decision.
Pacta sunt servanda: Agreements must be kept—promises are binding.
Pactum de non petendo: An agreement not to sue—a covenant not to sue.
Pandectae: The Digest—a compilation of Roman law.
Par in parem imperium non habet: Equals have no authority over equals.
Paralegal: A legal assistant—one who assists lawyers.
Parens patriae: Parent of the country—the state as guardian.
Pars pro toto: A part for the whole—representing the whole.
Partner: A co-owner—a member of a partnership.
Pater familias: The father of a family—the head of a household.
Paternity: Fatherhood—the state of being a father.
Patriot: One who loves his country—a patriot.
Penny: A coin—a small amount of money.
Per curiam: By the court—an opinion by the court as a whole.
Personality: Individuality—the quality of being a person.
Philosophy: Love of wisdom—the study of knowledge.
Pirate: A sea robber—one who commits piracy.
Pleading: A formal allegation—a statement in a lawsuit.
Posse comitatus: The power of the county—the armed populace.
Predecessor: One who came before—a prior holder.
Preempt: To take before—to acquire by preemption.
Prima facie: At first sight—on the face of it.
Pro forma: For form—as a matter of form.
Probate: Proving a will—the process of proving a will.
Promissory: Containing a promise—relating to a promise.
Prosecution: The bringing of criminal charges—the legal action.
Prosecutor: One who prosecutes—the lawyer for the state.
Quantum meruit: As much as he deserves—reasonable value for services.
Quantum valebant: As much as they were worth—reasonable value.
Quaternion: A set of four—a group of four.
Question: An inquiry—a doubt.
Qui facit per alium facit per se: He who acts through another acts himself—vicarious liability.
Qui prior est tempore, potior est jure: He who is first in time is stronger in law—priority in time gives priority in right.
Qui tacet consentire videtur: He who is silent appears to consent—silence implies consent.
Qui tam: Who as well—an action brought in part for the state.
Quo warranto: By what authority—a writ to determine the right to hold office.
Rape: The crime of forced sexual intercourse.
Ratio decidendi: The reason for deciding—the legal principle underlying a decision.
Ratio legis: The reason of the law—the purpose behind a law.
Receipt: A written acknowledgment—a proof of payment.
Receiver: A person appointed to receive—a custodian.
Relict: A surviving spouse—a widow or widower.
Replevin: An action to recover property—a legal proceeding.
Reputation: Opinion held of a person—public estimation.
Res ipsa loquitur: The thing speaks for itself—the facts imply negligence.
Res judicata: A matter adjudged—a case already decided.
Res nullius: A thing belonging to no one—ownerless property.
Resale: A second sale—the act of selling again.
Resident: One who lives in a place—an inhabitant.
Resort: A place of recourse—a vacation spot.
Respondent: The one who responds—a defendant in an appeal.
Riparian: Relating to a riverbank—pertaining to water rights.
Roman: Relating to Rome—pertaining to Roman law.
Scire facias: That you cause to know—a writ to enforce a judgment.
Sex: Gender—the state of being male or female.
Sheriff: A county officer—a law enforcement official.
Spoke: A rod—a part of a wheel.
Spouse: A married partner—a husband or wife.
Stare decisis: To stand by things decided—the doctrine of precedent.
Statute: A law—an act of the legislature.
Sub modo: With a limit—subject to a condition.
Sub nomine: Under the name—in the name of.
Subject: A topic—a person.
Subpoena: A writ to compel attendance—a summons.
Subrogation: The substitution of one person for another.
Sue: To bring legal action—to seek remedy.
Supersede: To replace—to take the place of.
Syllable: A unit of sound—a word part.
Taxation: The act of taxing—the system of taxes.
Tear: To rip—a drop from the eye.
Testamentary: Relating to a will—relating to testimony.
Testator: One who makes a will—a testator.
Throne: A chair of state—a seat of power.
Through: By means of—from end to end.
Tide: The rise and fall of the sea—a current.
Title: A name—a legal right.
Tort: A civil wrong—a breach of duty.
Trustee: One who holds property for another—a fiduciary.
Twin: One of two born together—a pair.
Uberrima fides: Utmost good faith—the duty of full disclosure.
Ubi jus ibi remedium: Where there is a right, there is a remedy—every right has a remedy.
Ubi lex non distinguit, nec nos distingu: Where the law does not distinguish, we ought not to distinguish.
Ultra vires: Beyond the powers—acting beyond legal authority.
Uncle: A brother of a parent—an adult male relative.
Upward: In a higher direction—toward the top.
Usury: Excessive interest—the practice of lending at illegal rates.
Uterine: Relating to the womb—brother by the same mother.
Venereal: Relating to sexual intercourse—relating to Venus.
Verdict: A decision of a jury—a finding.
Vis major: A greater force—an act of God.
Void ab initio: Void from the beginning—invalid from the outset.
Wade: To walk in water—to proceed slowly.
Week: A period of seven days—a week.
Widow: A woman whose husband is dead.
Widower: A man whose wife is dead.
Wing: A limb—a part of a building.
Year: A period of twelve months—a year.
Youth: The time of being young—a young person.
